name: Infer a gene regulatory network from single-cell expression
description: Which method infers a gene regulatory network from single-cell expression data that agrees with known regulation?

attributes.question: Which method infers a gene regulatory network from single-cell expression data that agrees with known regulation?
intended_users: Researchers inferring transcription factor to gene links from single-cell data
Method developers comparing network inference methods
attributes.decision: Choose a network inference method, and decide how far to trust the edges it ranks highest.
inputs: A single-cell expression matrix, optionally with chromatin accessibility
A list of candidate transcription factors
The reference network or held-out data the result will be judged against
attributes.output: Agreement of each method's ranked network with the reference, by the benchmark's own metrics, with the reference's kind stated.
attributes.setting: Research regulatory genomics. Reference networks differ in kind (ChIP-seq binding, perturbation response, curated literature), and a score against one does not transfer to another.
exclusions: Predicting expression after a perturbation, which has its own use case
Causal claims: agreement with a reference network does not establish that an edge is causal
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The linked evidence rests on one study, the geneRNIB result reported in the PerturbPFN paper. One study cannot settle the question.

The comparators in that result are recorded with origin paper_compilation, numbers the PerturbPFN paper copied from the geneRNIB leaderboard, so the board leaves them out and the use case has no comparison of two systems measured by one study yet.

BEELINE's results are in the store, recorded from three source-data files of one paper (Pratapa et al. 2020). They are one study, not three, although the store currently counts them as three because none of the three source records carries the paper's DOI in its doi field (docs/reviews/2026-11-27-use-case-mapping-gaps.md, section 8). Its 62 protocol records are not reviewed, so they are not linked.
No comparison of the same methods on the same data by two independent studies is linked.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

name: Choose a DNA language model for genomic element annotation

attributes.question: Which DNA language model, and which way of using it, classifies genomic elements such as promoters, enhancers, splice sites and histone marks most accurately for my sequences?
intended_users: Researchers choosing a DNA sequence model to annotate or classify regions of a genome
Method developers comparing a new DNA language model with published ones
attributes.decision: Choose a DNA language model, and whether to probe its frozen embeddings or fine-tune it, for a sequence annotation task.
inputs: DNA sequences of the element type of interest, with genome build and species
Labelled examples, or none if only a frozen probe is planned
A compute budget, which decides whether fine-tuning is possible
attributes.output: Per-task scores for each model under each training regime, with the task's split, kept separate by benchmark.
attributes.setting: Research genome annotation from sequence. Short-range and long-range tasks, frozen probes and fine-tuning are separate comparisons; a rank on one does not transfer to another.
exclusions: Variant effect prediction, which has its own use cases for missense, regulatory, rare-disease and splicing variants
Sequence conservation scores and synthetic promoter expression level, which are not element annotation
Pooling scores across benchmarks: each runs its own models, splits and probes
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The linked evidence rests on five studies: GenBench, the GENEB leaderboard, SegmentNT, the Nucleotide Transformer benchmark and GUANinE v1.1. The models they cover overlap only partly, so a model ranked well in one may be absent from the others.
BEND, DART-Eval, GUE, Genomic Benchmarks and Gene-MTEB results are in the store on task records with no protocol, so they cannot carry a judgement yet.
GENEB is recorded as two benchmark records, the leaderboard and GENEB, which are probably one benchmark.
No conventional baseline, such as a k-mer or position-weight-matrix classifier, is recorded as the reference these models must beat.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review, and nothing here was reproduced.

name: Annotate protein function from sequence

attributes.question: Which method assigns functions, such as Gene Ontology terms or enzyme classes, to protein sequences that have no close annotated relative?
intended_users: Researchers annotating proteins from a new genome, metagenome or design campaign
attributes.decision: Choose a function prediction method, and decide whether its accuracy is enough to annotate without manual curation.
inputs: Protein sequences
Whether close homologues with known function exist, which sets what a sequence-similarity baseline would achieve
attributes.output: Accuracy of each method on held-out proteins, separately for molecular function, biological process, cellular component and enzyme class.

Structure prediction, and function inferred from a predicted structure without a scored evaluation

No sequence-similarity baseline, such as BLAST transfer of the nearest annotated neighbour, is recorded as the reference these methods must beat.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review.

Method developers comparing protein language models as feature extractors

A split that reflects how the predictor will be used, such as holding out high-mutation or unseen-target sequences

FLIP, FLIP2, PFMBench, TAPE and the DeepProtein benchmark results are in the store but their protocol records are not reviewed, so the question has no second study linked.

name: Relevance of perturbpfn-20261115-protocol-genernib-300bcg-50k to use-case-gene-regulatory-network-inference
description: A submitted ranked transcription-factor-to-gene network scored by geneRNIB's official pipeline against held-out data, which is the use case's endpoint.

attributes.endpoint: Infer a weighted directed TF-gene network from 300BCG baseline profiles, submit at most 50,000 ranked links and score them with the official GeneRNIB pipeline on held-out profiles and external references.
attributes.rationale: A submitted ranked transcription-factor-to-gene network scored by geneRNIB's official pipeline against held-out data, which is the use case's endpoint.
constraints: Compare rows only within this protocol: GeneRNIB 300BCG GRN inference, 50,000-link budget, official all_metrics scoring (PerturbPFN Table 3).
limitations: The five baseline rows are copied from the official GeneRNIB score archive, not rerun by the PerturbPFN authors; the archive version and retrieval date are not stated (Appendix E.3).
Replicate consistency, a metric the official pipeline also reports, is omitted from Table 3 (Section 4.3).
PerturbPFN's graph is an intervention-propagation graph, not a curated GRN; the authors say it is related to but not identical to the regulatory references GeneRNIB scores against (Section 4.3).

attributes.endpoint: 3UTR: per-nucleotide annotation (auPRC). Scored with Area under precision-recall curve on Human genome 3UTR test chromosomes 20 and 21. Ten test-set samplings with sliding windows beginning at different genomic starting positions. Mean plus reported standard deviation; not ten training seeds. MCC and auPRC are separate metrics, not cross-element or cross-table pooled comparisons.

name: Relevance of segmentnt-supplement-2025-task-5utr-auprc to use-case-genomic-sequence-element-annotation
description: The task is to classify or annotate a genomic element from sequence, which is this use case's endpoint, with one score per model under a stated training regime.

attributes.endpoint: 5UTR: per-nucleotide annotation (auPRC). Scored with Area under precision-recall curve on Human genome 5UTR test chromosomes 20 and 21. Test chromosomes 20 and 21; validation chromosome 22; training remaining chromosomes. Test chunks with genes homologous to train/validation genes excluded using Ensembl BioMart accessed 2024-05-08; homologous distal regulatory elements not excluded. Ten test-set samplings with sliding windows beginning at different genomic starting positions. Mean plus reported standard deviation; not ten training seeds. Best validation checkpoint by average MCC across 14 elements. Per-nucleotide predictions pooled across test sequences separately for each genomic element. MCC and auPRC are separate metrics, not cross-element or cross-table pooled comparisons.

name: Relevance of glycangt-2026-table-s4-task-class-accuracy to use-case-glycan-property-prediction
description: A glycan property or taxonomic rank predicted from structure and scored by accuracy or macro-F1 on the GlycanML split, which is the use case's endpoint.

attributes.endpoint: GlycanGT study: class Accuracy. Scored with Accuracy on SugarBase taxonomy class; GlycanML official motif split. Taxonomy: 13,209 glycans total across eight levels, 4–1,737 classes per level. Official fixed GlycanML motif-based train/validation/test splits (8:1:1). Section 2.5 reports class-balanced classifiers, train ∪ validation hyperparameter selection by randomized search with 3-fold cross-validation, followed by one evaluation on the held-out test set; complete procedure repeated with three random seeds, reporting mean and standard deviation. GlycanGT large model pretrained with 35% masking provides [Graph] embeddings to SVM/LightGBM; the selected classifier for each S4 row is not identified. Section 2.6 states that all four graph baselines were trained and evaluated on the same datasets/splits; it does not establish that each baseline used the GlycanGT downstream classifier search. SVM search: 10 iterations, RBF/linear, C logU(1e-3,1e2), gamma logU(1e-4,1e-1); LightGBM: 15 randomized iterations. Do not combine with separate original GlycanML-paper protocols.

attributes.endpoint: R1107: RMSD. Scored with RMSD on CASP15 natural RNA target R1107. Retrospective evaluation of six CASP15 natural single-chain RNA targets; each task retains one named target.
